summary: Arabic numbers follow four rules by size. 1 and 2: the noun alone says it (كِتَابٌ a book, كِتَابَانِ two books — the dual); وَاحِد / اِثْنَانِ after the noun only stress the number, and they agree with it. 3–10: the number takes the OPPOSITE gender of the noun (gender polarity) and the noun follows in the genitive plural: ثَلَاثَةُ كُتُبٍ (كِتَاب is masculine → the number with ة), ثَلَاثُ غُرَفٍ (غُرْفَة is feminine → without ة). 11–99: the noun is accusative SINGULAR: أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كِتَابًا, عِشْرُونَ طَالِبًا. 100 and 1000: the noun is genitive singular: مِائَةُ كِتَابٍ, أَلْفُ شَخْصٍ. The number phrase itself takes the case of its place in the sentence (as the subject: عِشْرُونَ; after a preposition: عِشْرِينَ). As in German, 21–99 say the unit first: خَمْسَةٌ وَعِشْرُونَ = fünfundzwanzig.

blocks.caption: The gender that counts is the gender of the SINGULAR noun: بِنْت is feminine → ثَلَاثُ بَنَاتٍ; رَجُل is masculine → ثَلَاثَةُ رِجَالٍ.

blocks.caption: Counting aloud uses the forms with ة (ثَلَاثَة، أَرْبَعَة …). Digits are written left to right even inside Arabic text: ٢٠٢٦ = 2026. North Africa writes 0–9.

blocks.title: 3–10: the gender flips.
blocks.text: Masculine noun → the number WITH ة: ثَلَاثَةُ رِجَالٍ, خَمْسَةُ كُتُبٍ. Feminine noun → the number WITHOUT ة: ثَلَاثُ نِسَاءٍ, خَمْسُ غُرَفٍ. In this course's tables MASC / FEM on a number means the gender of the noun it counts.

blocks.title: After 11 the noun is singular again.
blocks.text: عِشْرُونَ طَالِبًا (twenty students — literally “twenty as to student”), not *عِشْرُونَ طُلَّابًا. The accusative -an is the sign: كِتَابًا, غُرْفَةً, كُرْسِيًّا.

blocks.title: Numbers that change for case.
blocks.text: The tens: عِشْرُونَ (subject) / عِشْرِينَ (object, after a preposition). Twelve: اِثْنَا عَشَرَ / اِثْنَيْ عَشَرَ. Two: اِثْنَانِ / اِثْنَيْنِ. Eight with feminine nouns: ثَمَانِي غُرَفٍ (nom., gen.), ثَمَانِيَ غُرَفٍ (acc.). The other teens never change: ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ.

items: the case of the whole phrase

blocks.text: 21–99 are built unit + وَ + ten, like German: وَاحِدٌ وَعِشْرُونَ (21, einundzwanzig), خَمْسَةٌ وَثَلَاثُونَ (35). The unit follows the 3–10 rule for gender; the counted noun is accusative singular: خَمْسَةٌ وَعِشْرُونَ طَالِبًا.
In everyday speech the case endings disappear (ʿišrīn instead of ʿišrūna), but the shape of the rules — plural after 3–10, singular after 11 — is the same in the dialects.

blocks.title: Ask yourself before you count
questions: What is the gender of the noun in the SINGULAR?
Genitive plural, accusative singular, or genitive singular after it?
Is the number phrase the subject (nominative) or not?

askYourself: 1 or 2? → the noun alone, singular or dual (كِتَابٌ, كِتَابَانِ); وَاحِد / اِثْنَانِ after it only for emphasis, agreeing.
3–10? → what is the gender of the SINGULAR noun? Masculine → the number with ة; feminine → without. Then the noun in the genitive plural.
11–99? → the noun in the accusative singular (-an). 11 and 12 agree; in 13–19 the unit flips and the ten agrees; the tens have no gender.
100 or 1000? → the noun in the genitive singular.
What is the case of the whole number phrase in the sentence (subject → nominative: عِشْرُونَ, اِثْنَا عَشَرَ)?

traps: *ثَلَاثُ كُتُبٍ is wrong: كِتَاب is masculine → ثَلَاثَةُ كُتُبٍ.
The gender comes from the singular, not from how the plural looks: بِنْت (f.) → ثَلَاثُ بَنَاتٍ; رَجُل (m.) → ثَلَاثَةُ رِجَالٍ.
After 11–99 the noun is singular: عِشْرُونَ طَالِبًا, not *عِشْرُونَ طُلَّابًا.
“Two books” is the dual كِتَابَانِ, not *اِثْنَانِ كِتَابٌ.
The tens have no gender: عِشْرُونَ بِنْتًا, عِشْرُونَ وَلَدًا.
100 and 1000 take the singular: مِائَةُ طَالِبٍ, not *مِائَةُ طُلَّابٍ.

quiz.why: 3–10 flip the gender: a masculine noun takes the number with ة, and the noun is genitive plural.
Feminine noun → the number without ة; genitive plural بَنَاتٍ.
11–99: the noun is singular and accusative (-an).
Two of something is the dual of the noun itself.
After 100 and 1000 the noun is genitive singular.
The unit first, then “and” and the ten — like German fünfundzwanzig.
13–19: the unit flips (خَمْسَ for a feminine noun), the ten agrees (عَشْرَةَ), the noun is accusative singular.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew has the same reversed gender for 3–10 (שְׁלוֹשָׁה סְפָרִים / שָׁלוֹשׁ בָּנוֹת), but no cases, and the noun stays plural after 11 and above.
German numbers hardly change (only ein / eine), but 21–99 put the unit first as in Arabic: einundzwanzig = وَاحِدٌ وَعِشْرُونَ.
Chinese puts a measure word between the number and the noun (三本书) and has two words for “two” (二 / 两); Arabic changes the noun's number and case instead.
The counted noun after 3–10 is the plural you learn with each noun — often a broken plural.

notes.text: Greek changes only 1, 3, 4 (and the hundreds) for gender, and after 2 the noun is always plural (τρία βιβλία); Arabic reverses the gender of 3–10, uses the dual for 2 and a singular after 10. Greek says the tens first (είκοσι ένα), Arabic the unit first (وَاحِدٌ وَعِشْرُونَ).

Russian also changes the noun with the number — два стола, пять столов; Arabic has its own steps: the dual for 2, the genitive plural for 3–10, the accusative singular for 11–99, the genitive singular for 100. Russian says the tens first (двадцать один).

Spanish numbers barely change (uno / una, doscientos / doscientas) and the noun is plural after 2; Arabic reverses the gender of 3–10 and uses the singular after 10. Spanish says the tens first (veintiuno).

In English only the noun’s -s changes; Arabic has a dual for 2, reversed gender for 3–10, the singular after 11–99 (عِشْرُونَ طَالِبًا, “twenty student”), and the unit before the ten in 21–99, as in old “four-and-twenty”.
French counts 70 and 80 in twenties (soixante-dix, quatre-vingts) and says the tens first (vingt et un); Arabic is decimal throughout and says the unit first (وَاحِدٌ وَعِشْرُونَ).
Hindi 21–99 are fused words with the unit first, to be learned one by one (पच्चीस, 25); Arabic builds them in the same order but regularly: unit + وَ + ten (خَمْسَةٌ وَعِشْرُونَ).
Persian keeps the noun singular after every number (سه کتاب, “three book”); Arabic uses the plural after 3–10 and the singular from 11. Persian says the tens first (بیست و یک).
Marathi 21–99 are, like Hindi ones, single words with the unit first (पंचवीस, 25); Arabic builds them as unit + وَ + ten.

Turkish keeps the noun singular after any number (üç kitap); Arabic uses a genitive plural after 3–10 (ثَلَاثَةُ كُتُبٍ) and an accusative singular after 11–99. Turkish says the tens first (yirmi bir).
Japanese needs a counter between number and noun (三冊の本); Arabic needs none, but the number itself changes gender (ثَلَاثَةُ كُتُبٍ, ثَلَاثُ غُرَفٍ).
Korean needs a counter (책 세 권) and has two sets of numbers; Arabic has one set, no counters, and reversed gender for 3–10.
Finnish puts a singular noun in the partitive after numbers (kolme kirjaa); Arabic does something similar only from 11 (أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كِتَابًا) and uses the plural for 3–10.
Hungarian keeps the noun singular after numbers (három könyv); Arabic uses the dual for 2 and the plural for 3–10.
Swahili puts the number after the noun and makes it agree by class (vitabu vitatu); Arabic puts 3–10 before the noun and gives them the opposite gender (ثَلَاثَةُ كُتُبٍ).
Luganda numbers follow the noun and agree by class (ebitabo bisatu, three books); Arabic 3–10 come first and take the opposite gender of the noun.
Vietnamese needs a classifier (ba quyển sách) and leaves the noun unchanged; Arabic has no classifier but changes the noun’s number and case after each number.
Inuktitut nouns have a dual too, so “two” can be said by the noun alone — as Arabic كِتَابَانِ is “two books”.
